column4: The aim of reperfusion is the timely restoration of coronary flow.  Primary PCI is preferred for reperfusion therapy in patients with STEMI if it can be performed within 90 minutes of first medical contact (diagnosis)2.
column5:
The rationale for measuring this indicator is based on the principle of "time is muscle," which refers to the fact that the longer it takes to restore blood flow to the heart during a heart attack, the more damage is done to the heart muscle.

In cases of STEMI, rapid restoration of blood flow is crucial to limit the size of the infarcted area and prevent further damage to the heart. Guidelines recommend that patients with STEMI undergo PCI within 90 minutes of their first medical contact, or within 120 minutes if they need to be transferred to a PCI-capable hospital. Measuring the time from diagnostic ECG to PCI-mediated reperfusion allows hospitals to evaluate how quickly they are able to provide this life-saving treatment to their patients and identify areas for improvement in their processes of care

column2: Time from door to PCI mediated reperfusion
column3: The time from the patient's presentation to the PCI room and completed reperfusion via coronary intervention.
column4: Reperfusion treatment for patients with STEMI is time critical and excessive delays can have serious adverse impacts on patient outcomes.
column5:
The rationale for measuring this indicator is that it reflects the time it takes for patients to receive appropriate treatment from the time they arrive at the hospital, and can help to identify delays in the care process that may impact patient outcomes.

Delays in the care process can occur at multiple stages, such as delays in recognizing symptoms, transport to the hospital, triage in the emergency department, and activation of the cardiac catheterization team. Guidelines recommend that patients with STEMI receive primary PCI within 90 minutes of arriving at the hospital, or within 120 minutes if they need to be transferred to a PCI-capable hospital.

Measuring the time from door to PCI-mediated reperfusion allows hospitals to evaluate how quickly they are able to provide this life-saving treatment to their patients and identify areas for improvement in their processes of care. This indicator can also be useful for tracking changes over time and comparing performance across different hospitals or healthcare systems.

It is important to note, however, that this indicator should be used in conjunction with other measures of quality of care for PCI, such as procedural success rates, complication rates, and long-term outcomes for patients.

Peri-PCI stroke is a potential complication of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and refers to a stroke that occurs during or immediately after the procedure. The rationale for measuring the rate of peri-PCI stroke is to assess the safety of the procedure and to identify areas for improvement in preventing this serious complication.

PCI is a common procedure for treating coronary artery disease, but it carries a small risk of stroke. Factors that may increase the risk of peri-PCI stroke include advanced age, previous stroke or transient ischemic attack, high blood pressure, diabetes, and complex or lengthy procedures.

Measuring the rate of peri-PCI stroke can help hospitals and healthcare systems to monitor the safety of their PCI procedures and identify any factors that may be contributing to an increased risk of stroke. This indicator can also be used to compare performance across different hospitals or healthcare systems, and to evaluate the effectiveness of quality improvement initiatives aimed at reducing the incidence of peri-PCI stroke.

It is important to note that while the rate of peri-PCI stroke is an important measure of quality of care, it should be interpreted in the context of other measures of PCI safety and effectiveness, such as procedural success rates, complication rates, and long-term outcomes for patients.

In-hospital mortality is a crucial outcome measure for patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and refers to death occurring during the hospitalization for the procedure. The rationale for measuring the rate of in-hospital mortality is to evaluate the effectiveness of PCI procedures and to identify areas for improvement in patient care and outcomes.

PCI is a common procedure for treating coronary artery disease, but it carries a small risk of complications, including death. Factors that may increase the risk of in-hospital mortality include advanced age, heart failure, diabetes, and severe coronary artery disease.

Measuring the rate of in-hospital mortality allows hospitals and healthcare systems to monitor the effectiveness of their PCI procedures and identify any factors that may be contributing to an increased risk of mortality. This indicator can also be used to compare performance across different hospitals or healthcare systems and to evaluate the effectiveness of quality improvement initiatives aimed at reducing the incidence of in-hospital mortality.

It is important to note that while the rate of in-hospital mortality is an important measure of quality of care, it should be interpreted in the context of other measures of PCI safety and effectiveness, such as procedural success rates, complication rates, and long-term outcomes for patients. Additionally, it is essential to consider the severity of illness and comorbidities of the patient population undergoing PCI, as these factors can significantly influence the rate of in-hospital mortality.
